disagreements.topic: Who decides what gets built: the PM as CEO of the product, the engineer, or a cross-functional trio?

positions.claim: The PM is 'the CEO of the product': defines the what, manages the product team, takes full responsibility for outcomes; the PM owns value and viability risk.
The PM is not the CEO: no authority over design, engineering, marketing, sales; authority is earned and product management is a team sport.
Engineers run the product and manage the team; PMs are a compass (information and coaching) and do not own the roadmap. At Linear engineers lead projects (rotating) with one PM in the company.

A trio/cross-functional team with split risk ownership (PM: value+viability, designer: usability, lead engineer: feasibility); in 2026 the PM is 'a builder, not a manager' who builds and tests prototypes.

AI makes building cheaper, so demand rises for people who write clear specs of what to build; typical Engineer:PM ratio is about 6:1 today (4:1 to 10:1 range) and strong PMs are expected to prototype themselves.
Shaping needs a generalist or one to two collaborators; the Shape Up pages name no PM (betting table: CEO, CTO, senior programmer, product strategist).

disagreements.topic: How should discovery be done: weekly interviews, prototypes, experiments, or shape-and-bet?

positions.claim: Continuous discovery: interview customers every week, map opportunities in an opportunity solution tree, compare more than one solution per opportunity, test assumptions. PostHog's PM rule of thumb is 1 interview per week per PM.
Discovery is mostly prototypes by the product team, at least an order of magnitude cheaper than building, iterated 3-5 times before delivery.

Randomized controlled experiments are the arbiter, but most ideas fail (1/3, 10-20%, ~30%, '90% wrong' depending on domain), so test everything and use complementary techniques (logs, surveys, UER) where experiments cannot run; metrics are not a substitute for formative user research.
Shape then bet: no customer-research cadence prescribed; ideas that matter 'come back'; shaping is rough, solved and bounded work done before betting.
Write the customer announcement and FAQ first; vet the idea in writing before assigning engineers.

disagreements.topic: What is the right spec artifact: PRD, prototype, pitch, PR/FAQ, or a short project spec?

positions.claim: A ten-step PRD is the highest-leverage document and drives the whole company (2005).
The prototype is the spec; the PRD only carries use cases and non-functional requirements a prototype cannot show (2026).
A pitch (problem, appetite, solution sketch, rabbit holes, no-gos) at deliberately low fidelity: do not over-specify with wireframes or high-fidelity mocks.
A PR/FAQ written backwards from the customer announcement; first draft in a few hours.
A concise 1-2 page project spec for situational awareness, plus engineers deciding readiness without a checklist document.
As building gets cheaper, clear written specs gain value and PMs are expected to prototype as well.

disagreements.topic: Roadmaps and backlogs: reshape, abolish or keep?

positions.claim: Replace feature roadmaps with vision, prioritized business objectives and OKRs; give dates only as high-integrity commitments that cost discovery work and are used sparingly.
No backlog and no central list; bet six weeks at a time with a two-week cool-down; circuit breaker kills unfinished work by default; two-week cycles are too short.
Keep a manageable backlog and let low-priority items die; two-week cycles are most common; keep a roadmap of themes for about six months and project end dates.

disagreements.topic: Prioritization: estimate and rank, set an appetite and bet, or let attrition filter?

positions.claim: Score by Reach x Impact x Confidence / Effort (person-months), with the author's own caveat that it is not a hard rule.
Appetites start with a number and end with a design; estimates start with a design and end with a number; over-specified work is harder to estimate.
Do not keep every request: important ones resurface, low-priority ones never get fixed.
Let measured idea success rates (1/3 or lower) decide: the Bing change that sat six months in the backlog was worth over $100M/year, so a prior ranking can be badly wrong.

Prioritize by economics: quantify cost of delay in money and sequence by it; FIFO ordering is almost never optimal in product development; where cost of delay is not calculated, answers for the same project vary by 50 to 1 (course-survey statistics: only 15% of developers know their cost of delay).

disagreements.topic: Evidence vs judgment: how much data before acting?

positions.claim: Be data-driven: formalize an OEC, run controlled experiments, let data inform the HiPPO; the organization is poor at assessing the value of ideas.
Decide at about 70% of the information you wish you had; disagree and commit; beware proxies such as process, surveys and beta-test averages standing in for customers.
Apple under Steve Jobs is cited as the notable organization that did not test ads at all.
Metrics must be tied to goals first and triangulated with qualitative research; they evaluate launched products and do not replace formative research.

disagreements.topic: Aligning teams to goals: OKRs, a single OEC with guardrails, initiatives, or bets?

positions.claim: OKRs: three to five objectives, about three key results each, graded 0.0-1.0 with a 0.6-0.7 target, public, not an evaluation tool; Cagan's 'current favorite'.
A single composite OEC, measurable in one to two weeks and predictive of long-term goals, plus guardrails for what must not degrade; 'percent of plan delivered' is a poor key metric.
Product initiatives plus a product timeline (Linear); no OKR mention on the fetched pages (silence, not opposition).
Appetite-bounded bets with no goal-tracking apparatus on the fetched chapters.

disagreements.topic: Personas or jobs-to-be-done for understanding users?

positions.claim: Build demographic personas (e.g., 'Leon the Power Seller is a 46 year old male ...') as design archetypes.
Segments by product category or demographics correlate with but do not cause purchase; interview for the job the customer hires the product to do.
Map opportunities as customer needs, pain points and desires under a product outcome, interviewing weekly.
Understanding customer jobs, not understanding customers, drives innovation success (the publisher's statement of the book's thesis; mechanism not fetched).

disagreements.topic: Pricing a developer or infrastructure product

positions.claim: Usage-based as the default, no per-extra-user fee, match the cheapest big competitor that makes real revenue at scale, generous but bounded free tier, free tier is a one-way door, yearly pricing review.

Flat per-seat is simple but does not reflect compute cost; usage-based costs predictability and may slow adoption; hybrid (seat + usage) keeps both; flat seat plus heavy agentic usage 'will eventually create a margin problem'.
Push down the price of complements to your product, so pricing power comes from controlling the stack around you.

disagreements.topic: Speed of change vs user trust (relevant to ML features that adapt over time)

positions.claim: Run a very large volume of experiments and iterate quickly; most big redesigns fail but cheap incremental tests pay off.
Change aversion is real: satisfaction dropped after a redesign and recovered.
'Update and adapt cautiously'; limit disruptive changes when the AI system adapts.
'If you release something and iterate too much, it can be difficult for your customers'; Cagan warns of 'constant, erratic change'.

disagreements.topic: What a strategy is and where product strategy comes from

positions.claim: Strategy should not be equated with ambition, leadership, vision or planning (publisher's statement of the book's thesis; the kernel itself was not fetched).
Product vision plus prioritized business objectives per team, expressed as OKRs, replace the feature roadmap as the statement of direction.
Strategy is encoded in the OEC: the strategy drives the choice of OEC, guardrails state what the organization will not trade away, and experiments hill-climb within it.
Strategy is positional economics: commoditize the complements of your product so demand for it rises.
